On my first morning at the lost property office, a man came looking for a cake. He had left it on the number six bus, in a white box tied with string. It was his daughter's birthday. The driver had already brought it in, but I was new enough to insist on proof. What kind of cake? I asked. He considered this. “Disappointing,” he said. “I tried to make a horse.” We opened the box together. The animal had sunk in the middle and appeared to be kneeling in prayer. I handed it over. He thanked me without meeting my eyes.

Most things that arrived at our counter had suffered some small indignity. Umbrellas turned inside out. A violin case bore the tread of a remarkably narrow bicycle tire. Someone had used a paperback dictionary to mop up coffee; from P onward the language was inaccessible. My colleague June taught me to record these injuries without guessing at their causes. Write “brown stain,” she said, not “coffee.” Write “cover detached,” not “badly loved.” I had never written “badly loved,” but apparently someone once had. June had worked there for thirty years and retained a precise memory of every interesting mistake except her own.

In November we received a wooden drawer. Nothing else, just one kitchen drawer, painted yellow, with a porcelain knob and a sheet of green paper lining the bottom. It came off the last train on a Thursday night. I entered it under Furniture, which until then had consisted entirely of folding chairs. For several days we discussed the person who had lost it. June thought a cabinetmaker was matching paint. The cleaner thought somebody had been evicted in stages. My own theory involved a magician, though I could not say what particular trick required a drawer that stuck slightly when pushed.

People began leaving things in it. A delivery driver put his pen there while he signed for a parcel, then went away without it. June dropped in a brass button she found beside the lift. I contributed three rubber bands and a key to a padlock we no longer owned. By December, without anybody intending it, the drawer had resumed its occupation. If you needed string, a safety pin, or a coin from a country that had since adopted the euro, there was only one sensible place to look. We stopped thinking of it as lost property. It was simply the drawer.

Then a woman arrived with a photograph of a kitchen. I recognized the yellow paint before she spoke. In the photograph a boy stood on a chair rolling pastry, his sleeves pushed up unevenly. Behind him, at hip height, there was a dark rectangular gap. “My brother,” the woman said, pointing to the boy. “I took this the day before they pulled the house down.” She had meant to keep one thing from the kitchen and had chosen the drawer because their father had made it. On the way home she changed trains twice. Somewhere she had set it down.

I fetched it from under the counter. We had acquired rather a lot of things by then. As I tipped them onto my blotter, out came a candle shaped like a seven, two curtain hooks, a dog whistle, and a folded recipe for onion soup in June's handwriting. The woman laughed. “That's about right,” she said. She ran her thumb along the inside edge and showed me a shallow notch. As children they had closed the drawer on a length of wool leading down the hall, to see whether their sleeping father would notice when his kitchen began to unravel.

“Did he?” I asked. “Of course. We were pulling a drawer across the floor.” She tucked it beneath her arm. There should have been a satisfying noise when the office door closed behind her, but the pneumatic hinge had been adjusted that morning, and she left us in perfect silence. For the rest of the afternoon we worked around the little heap on my desk. Twice I reached underneath the counter for the drawer. June put the curtain hooks in her pocket. At five she unfolded the recipe and discovered it was not onion soup after all, but instructions for descaling a kettle.

I thought of buying another drawer. There was a furniture shop near my flat that sold salvaged fittings, and on Saturday I went in. The owner showed me six. One was walnut, with dovetailed corners so fine they resembled a diagram explaining the idea of precision to beginners. Another smelled of cloves. I slid them in and out of their cabinets while the owner stood by, politely enduring the least consequential decision of his working week. Finally he asked what dimensions I needed. I admitted that I had nothing to fit the drawer into. “Ah,” he said. “Much greater choice, then.”

I went home empty-handed. On Monday the heap was gone. June had used the rubber bands to bundle some timetables, given the whistle to a crossing guard, and put the birthday candle in an envelope marked SEVEN, OR POSSIBLY SEVENTY IF YOU HAVE A ZERO. The pen had been claimed by the delivery driver, who said it was the only pen in the city that worked in the rain. I asked about the useless key. June pointed to the violin case with the bicycle mark. Its owner was coming at lunchtime, and one of the catches needed persuading from underneath.

Years later, what I remember best about that office is how often a person, reunited with a possession, immediately put it to work. A scarf went around a neck. A watch was wound and consulted. The violinist took out her bow, tightened it, and played four notes before she even signed the form. They were not especially lovely notes. She was listening for damage, and so were we. The last note wavered, steadied, then filled the little room where June and I stood holding our breath, each of us, for once, quite certain what the other had been hoping to hear.
